units.title: Holm timber camp: wages book of J. Penhallow (1894)
units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Transcriber's note: the wages book is a separate volume from the tally book, bound in green cloth, water-stained at the lower edge. Oct 31st 1894. Paid to the end of October. Fourteen men at 3s. 2d. per diem less board at 9d. Cook at 2s. 6d. and found. Boy (Jno. Pascoe) 1s. 4d. Horses' keep entered under stores. All paid in silver and copper, none wanting.

units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Oct 31st, continued. Deductions this month: T. Gale 2s. for a lost wedge, which he disputes, and it is enterd as disputed. W. Hosken 1s. 6d. advanced against tobacco. Rd. Treloar fined 6d. for a fire left burning in the bunkhouse stove at night, by order of Mr. Varcoe. The men took it in good part. Total wages for the month, 71l. 8s. 4d.

units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Nov 7th. Advances this week against November wages: Hosken 1s. tobacco, Gale 2s. 6d. to send home by the boat, Pascoe the boy 6d. for a knife, which I am told he has already lost. Cook asks for an extra 1s. for having fed the boatmen twice in the fog when they could not get off. Allowed by Mr. Varcoe. Weather thick all week.

units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Nov 7th, memorandum. Mr. Varcoe directs that a man who will work the far lines on the north end shall have 2d. per diem over the rate, the ground being bad and the walk long. Four men put their names down. Three more said they would think on it. Entered as directed. Lamp oil, two gallons, charged to the camp.

units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Nov 10th. Gale's wedge found under the sledge road by the boy, and his 2s. returned to him with apology, he being right and I being wrong. Let it be recorded. The men stood him a pipe of tobacco for his patience. Fog still on the water. The boat came late in the afternoon and lay off till it could see the landing.

units.title: Carrow Point light: log extracts (December 1904)
units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Middle watch, 2 Dec 1904. 00:00 Lamp lit and burning well. Wind E 2, visibility 4 miles, cold. 01:10 trimmed wicks. 02:00 steamer passing west, lights correct, gave no signal. 03:00 visibility falling, mist on the water. 03:40 visibility under a mile. 04:00 relieved by assistant keeper. Remarks: nil.

units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Middle watch, 3 Dec 1904. 00:00 Lamp burning well. Wind calm. Thick fog, visibility under a cable. 00:05 fog signal started, engine running sweet. 01:30 lamp glass running wet, wiped down twice. 03:00 no vessels heard. Remarks: fog signal ran the full watch. Coal for engine, four scuttles.

units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Middle watch, 4 Dec 1904. 00:00 Lamp burning well. Calm, fog continuing. Fog signal working without fault. 02:15 a ship's bell heard to the south-west, faint, answered by our signal. 02:50 bell no longer heard. 04:00 relieved. Remarks: engine bearing warm, oiled, to be watched.

units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Middle watch, 6 Dec 1904. 00:00 Lamp burning well. Wind SW 1, fog thinning by turns. 01:00 lights of Gilliver seen for some minutes, then lost. 02:30 visibility 2 miles, fog signal stopped 02:34. 03:10 fog returned, signal restarted 03:12. Remarks: assistant keeper's lad poorly with a cough. Sent for syrup by the carrier.

units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Middle watch, 8 Dec 1904. 00:00 Lamp burning well. Wind W 3, fog cleared, visibility 8 miles, stars. 01:20 trimmed wicks. 02:00 three fishing boats from Gilliver passing out, lights correct. 03:30 heavy dew on the gallery rail. Remarks: fog signal engine stood down and cleaned after six days' near constant work.

units.title: Notebook of Miss H. Arnell: Kittering Holm, June 1923
units.author: naturalist_1923
units.text: Kittering Holm, 7 June. Mr. P. landed me at eight, departed at once, returns at five. Shore list: oystercatcher 6 pr., common sandpiper 2, eider (rafts of 20 off the point), black guillemot. Woodland edge: chiffchaff singing, willow warbler, wren everywhere, a treecreeper on the big spruce. (Sketch: the spruce, with treecreeper, not to scale.)

units.author: naturalist_1923
units.text: 7 June, plants. Woodrush abundant under the spruce; wood sorrel; a very fine stand of the small fern I am calling Polypodium insulare until someone cleverer corrects me. Hazel and rowan along the burn heavily in leaf and, I note, quite unbrowsed, the lower twigs as whole as a hedge in a parson's garden.

units.author: naturalist_1923
units.text: 8 June. Fog, no crossing. Wrote up at the inn. The landlady informs me that Mr. P. has told the bar I am 'a woman who looks under stones', which is accurate. Later, clearing: walked to Gilliver harbour wall and counted 41 kittiwakes on the old curing station roof across the water with the long glass.

units.author: naturalist_1923
units.text: 9 June. Holm again. Mr. P. on time, which I record in fairness. North shore: ringed plover on the shingle, rock pipit, a pair of ravens working the ridge. Tried the gullies for small mammals with the traps; bank vole 2, wood mouse 1, all released. A heron stood all day at the burn mouth and did not move when I passed.

units.title: Diary of Amos Rendle, Gilliver: February 1934
units.author: fisher_diary_1930s
units.text: Feb 2. Fog. Did not go out. Father says its the worst start to Feb he can mind. Mended creels in the shed. Mother made pasties and sent one to old Mrs Tull who is poorly. Paid 4s to the chandler on account. Ling 5d, cod 4d at Ammet Saturday, not worth the carrying.

units.author: fisher_diary_1930s
units.text: Feb 4. Still fog. Went down the harbour at dark to see to the boat. Couldnt see the end of the slip from the top of it. Jack Pascoe was there with his lantern doing the same so we walked back up together. Mother had the lamp in the window as always. Bed at nine.

units.author: fisher_diary_1930s
units.text: Feb 7. Fog lifted at noon. Out at one with Father to the near ground, back by dark. Nine baskets. Lost two creels on the Holm side, the rope cut clean, rocks I suppose. Father would not go round the point to look for them though there was light enough. Said leave it.

units.author: fisher_diary_1930s
units.text: Feb 9. Fine and cold. Out at 5. Eighteen baskets, a good haul at last. Sold at Ammet, cod up to 6d. Bought Mother a new wick and a tin of oil and sister a ribbon. Treloar boy got his finger in a winch and is to have it seen to. Fog back by evening.

units.author: fisher_diary_1930s
units.text: Feb 12. Blowing from the west at last and the fog gone. Out at 4. Fourteen baskets. Found one of our lost creels washed up by the curing station steps, rope frayed not cut, so I was wrong about that. Father said nothing. Chapel tea at night, too many buns.

units.title: From the archive: the Sound fog of 1963
units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: Editor's note: with fog forecast this week, readers have asked about the great fog of November 1963, which some remember as lasting a fortnight. Our pages say nine days. The report below is from the Courier of 21 November 1963, page 1. The ferry figures are as printed; we have no means of checking them now.

units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: SOUND STILL BLIND ON SEVENTH DAY. The fog which descended upon the Marrow Sound last Thursday shows no sign of lifting. The car ferry has made only eleven of its scheduled forty crossings, and on Tuesday lay off Lisle for four hours unable to find the pier. Coal for Gilliver is being brought round by lorry.

units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: Continued. The Carrow Point keepers report that their fog signal has sounded for 150 hours without pause, a record for the station. At Brackwater, the reservoir works were stopped when the engineers could not see the far bank. A Tollinby farmer reports that his cows walked home on their own and waited at the gate.

units.title: From the archive: Lisle school closed by fog (1991)
units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: Editor's note: This week's fog coverage referred to the Lisle school closing for four days. Our own back issues say three. This brief appeared in the Courier of 14 November 1991, page 5. The teacher quoted retired some years later and still writes to us about our grammar.

units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: Lisle Primary School remained closed for a third day yesterday as fog stopped the ferry carrying its four mainland teachers. The head teacher, who lives on the island, kept the building open for parents who needed it and taught all three classes in the hall. 'We did fractions and the history of the island,' she said. 'Fractions went less well.'

units.title: Our Gilliver Correspondent: December 1894
units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: Editor's note: this column falls between the November and January columns already reproduced. Its date line reads 'December', with no day, and its account of the camp is more cheerful than the January column, which reports the men returning 'in poor spirits'. We print it as it stands.

units.author: courier_1890s
units.text: The fog that lay upon us for the better part of a week has at last withdrawn, and the timber boat has resumed her passages to the Holm. Her master reports the woodmen in health and good heart, though he says they were most eager for news and for tobacco, the latter having run short.

units.author: courier_1890s
units.text: The chapel Christmas sale realised four pounds and some shillings, chiefly by the sale of Mrs. Pascoe's jams. A collection was also made for the woodmen, and a box of comforts went over on the Tuesday boat. It is said that one of the men has written to his mother that the island is very quiet. We should think it is.

units.title: LB-0158: Sound Lines ferry, engine room, night crossing
units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LB-0158. Date: 7 February 1999. Location: engine room of the night ferry, Port Ammet to Lisle. Kit: DAT recorder, two dynamic mics taped to a handrail. Duration: 41 min. Description: twin diesels at steady load, a gearbox whine, the chief's radio in the background. Curator's note: recorded with permission; the recordist was the chief's nephew.

units.title: LB-0265: Brackwater Reservoir, ice settling
units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LB-0265. Date: 18 January 1991. Location: Brackwater Reservoir, east bank, below the fen gate. Kit: portable cassette, contact microphone on a stake frozen into the ice. Duration: 19 min. Description: long singing tones, cracks and booms as the ice sheet settles at dusk. Curator's note: often requested; frequently mistaken for whale song by people who have never heard either.

units.title: LB-0289: Weyhaven canal towpath, 2 a.m.
units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LB-0289. Date: 30 September 1993. Location: Canal Street towpath, Weyhaven, by the lock. Kit: minidisc, stereo pair. Duration: 26 min. Description: water over the lock gate, a distant freight train, a bicycle passing at 11:40, two people talking in another language. Curator's note: the tower blocks behind the recordist reflect the train sound twice, which some listeners take for a second train.

units.title: LB-0312: Gilliver slipway, low water
units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LB-0312. Date: 22 August 1995. Location: Gilliver slipway, standing at the foot of the slip at low water springs. Kit: portable DAT, omni mic. Duration: 12 min. Description: weed popping in the sun, small waves at the slip end, gulls, a creel boat coming in at 09:15. Curator's note: a pleasant summer file, catalogued under 'harbour, daytime'.

units.title: LB-0336: tower block stairwell, children's echo game
units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LB-0336. Date: 5 July 1997. Location: stairwell of a Weyhaven tower block (not named by the recordist). Kit: minidisc, hand-held mic. Duration: 6 min. Description: children calling numbers down the stairwell and counting the echoes. Curator's note: a useful reference for stairwell reflections. The recordist reports at least four clear repeats from a single handclap.

units.title: LB-0371: Marrow Sound in fog, ferry signals
units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LB-0371. Date: 12 November 1982. Location: Lisle pier, end of the walkway. Kit: portable cassette, cardioid mic. Duration: 33 min. Description: dense fog; the car ferry's horn at two-minute intervals, approaching from the east; Carrow Point signal faintly behind. Curator's note: the ferry horn seems to move left and right before arrival. This is the fog, not the ferry.

units.title: Gilliver slipway
units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: The Gilliver slipway runs from Harbour Road into the north side of the harbour. A stone slip existed by 1880, used for hauling boats and landing the curing station's salt. It was lengthened and given a concrete surface in 1912 (Society holdings, parish minute book), and widened again in 1957 when the car ferry service began calling at Gilliver.

units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: Use. The slip has served as ferry berth, boat launch and informal promenade. Villagers have long walked to its end at dusk to watch the boats come in, a habit noted in the 1976 oral history (tape 2). The lower section is steep and weeded and has been the scene of several accidents; a handrail was added in 1971. [citation needed for the date of the handrail]

units.title: Talk: Gilliver slipway
units.author: hist_wiki_pell
units.text: The 1912 date rests on a minute that records money 'voted for the slip', not on any record that the work was done. Survey maps of 1919 still show the shorter stone slip. Either the work was delayed, or the surveyor did not bother to revisit. I suggest '1912 to 1920'. The 'informal promenade' is charming and uncited; tape 2 says 'we went down to see Father in', which is not a promenade.

units.title: Fog in the Marrow Sound
units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: The Marrow Sound is prone to advection fog in late autumn and spring, when moist air moves over cold water. Fogs of a week or more are recorded in 1894, 1904, 1934, 1963 and 1991 (Carrow Point logs; Courier). The 1963 fog is the longest in the printed record at nine days, though local memory often makes it a fortnight.

units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: Customs. Fog weeks are associated in Gilliver with a number of small practices: boats kept in, lamps lit early, bells rung at the chapel at fixed hours in the 1890s (citation needed). Children were warned not to go down to the slip in fog. The window lamp custom is treated in a separate article and is not, as is sometimes claimed, specifically a fog custom.

units.title: Gilliver Oral History Project, tape 6: Mr. J. Haddow
units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Q: You were a ferryman? JH: Deckhand first, then mate, on the old boat before the car ferry. Forty year on the water. Q: What was the worst of it? JH: Fog. Not storms. A storm you can see coming. Fog comes in like a cat under a door. You stand forward and listen, and you listen so hard you start hearing things.

units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Q: Hearing things? JH: Bells that aren't there. Your own name. [pause] Gulls, mostly. Everything in fog is a gull until it isn't. Q: Did you ever see anything? JH: People on the slip. Always. Folk coming down to meet the boat with a lantern, or with no lantern, the daft beggars. You'd shout to them to get back up.

units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Q: And did they? JH: Mostly. [laughs] My skipper, old Pender, he'd say if they don't answer, they're either deaf or drunk or courting, and none of them's our business. Q: The timber camp, did you ever carry those men? JH: Before my time. My father did. He said they were a cheerful lot going out. He never said coming back.

units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Q: Did he say anything about the Holm? JH: He said it was good timber and a bad landing, and that's what I'd say. Nothing to it. [pause] Mind, he never let us play on the Holm side of the harbour after tea. But my mother wouldn't let us play on the chapel side either, so make of that what you like.
